questions.stem: Why do the agar blocks start pink?

options.text: Sodium hydroxide makes the agar alkaline and phenolphthalein turns pink in alkali
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: The agar is naturally pink
options.explanation: The colour comes from the indicator, not the jelly.

options.text: The acid dyes the blocks
options.explanation: Acid is added later, outside the block.

options.text: Phenolphthalein is pink at all pH values
options.explanation: It is colourless below pH 8.3.

questions.stem: What causes the pink colour to disappear during the investigation?

options.text: The agar dissolves into the acid
options.explanation: The jelly stays solid while the colour moves inward.

options.text: Diffusing acid neutralises the alkali inside the block
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: The indicator evaporates from the surface
options.explanation: The change happens throughout the block.

options.text: Light bleaches the dye
options.explanation: Light plays no role in the reaction.

questions.stem: Which block loses its colour first, and why?

options.text: All blocks at the same time
options.explanation: The ratios differ, so the rates differ.

options.text: The block with the smallest surface
options.explanation: Area alone is not the measure — it is area per volume.

options.text: The smallest block, because its surface area to volume ratio is the highest
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: The largest block, because it holds more acid
options.explanation: Size does not draw acid in faster.

questions.stem: Which measurement apparatus is explicitly required when cutting the cubes?

options.text: A thermometer, to track temperature
options.explanation: Temperature is not the variable being cut.

options.text: A balance, to weigh the agar
options.explanation: Mass is not the controlled measure here.

options.text: A stopwatch only
options.explanation: Timing matters, but the cut accuracy needs the ruler and scalpel.

options.text: A ruler and a sharp scalpel, used to cut as accurately as possible
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

questions.stem: How does this agar model show the effect of surface area on diffusion rate?

options.text: By comparing how quickly differently sized blocks decolourise
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: By measuring how far the acid heats the blocks
options.explanation: No temperature change is involved.

options.text: By weighing the blocks before and after
options.explanation: Mass change is not the read-out.

options.text: By timing how fast the agar melts
options.explanation: The agar never melts during the test.

questions.stem: State the colours phenolphthalein shows in acidic and alkaline conditions.
questions.modelAnswer: It shows colourless in acidic mixtures below pH 8.3, turning pink once conditions turn alkaline.

questions.stem: Name the two substances mixed into molten agar for this practical.
questions.modelAnswer: Sodium hydroxide, an alkali, and phenolphthalein indicator.

questions.stem: Explain why the decolourised front moves inward rather than outward.
questions.modelAnswer: Because acid particles diffuse in from the surrounding solution, crossing the surface and reacting progressively deeper; the neutralisation therefore advances from the edge towards the centre as the gradient drives the acid inward.

questions.stem: A student doubles every dimension of a cube. Predict the effect on its surface area to volume ratio and on its decolourisation time.
questions.modelAnswer: Doubling each side multiplies surface area fourfold but volume eightfold, so the ratio halves and the acid needs longer to reach the centre, roughly doubling the time before the block turns colourless.

questions.stem: Why must each potato cylinder be blotted before weighing?

options.text: To sterilise the cylinder
options.explanation: Sterility is not the purpose of the paper towel.

options.text: To remove surface liquid that would add spurious mass
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: To start osmosis earlier
options.explanation: Blotting only dries the outside.

options.text: To remove the skin
options.explanation: The skin stays on; blotting removes droplets.

questions.stem: Which cylinder gains the most mass after soaking?

options.text: All cylinders gain equally
options.explanation: Each concentration gives a different gradient.

options.text: The one that was heaviest at the start
options.explanation: Starting mass does not decide the direction.

options.text: The one in distilled water, where the steepest gradient drives water in
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: The one in the strongest sucrose solution
options.explanation: There water leaves the cells instead.

questions.stem: What does a cylinder with no change in mass tell you?

options.text: Osmosis failed to happen
options.explanation: Water crossed both ways equally; osmosis still ran.

options.text: The cylinder was left in too long
options.explanation: Duration affects size of change, not its sign.

options.text: The balance was misread
options.explanation: A fair reading is assumed; the physics explains the null.

options.text: Its cells' concentration matched the surrounding solution, so there was no net water movement
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

questions.stem: Why is percentage change in mass used instead of raw mass change?

options.text: Cylinders differ slightly in starting mass, so percentages make results comparable
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Percentages are easier to add up
options.explanation: The purpose is fair comparison, not arithmetic ease.

options.text: Raw mass cannot be measured
options.explanation: The balance gives raw mass directly.

options.text: Percentages remove the need for repeats
options.explanation: Repeats are still required for reliability.

questions.stem: Which limitation is acknowledged about the potato cylinders, and what fix is applied?

options.text: Osmosis is too slow to observe, so heat is added
options.explanation: Four hours suffices; no heating is applied.

options.text: Slight cylinder differences reduce reliability, so each concentration is repeated several times
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Sugar is unsafe, so it is replaced
options.explanation: Sucrose solutions are used throughout.

options.text: Potatoes cannot be cut evenly, so none are used
options.explanation: Cylinders are cut as equally as possible and repeats handle the rest.

questions.stem: State the calculation used to analyse each cylinder's result.
questions.modelAnswer: The percentage change in mass of the cylinder after soaking.

questions.stem: Name the cells made soft and flaccid in strong solution.
questions.modelAnswer: The potato cells become plasmolysed as water leaves them and the membrane pulls from the wall.

questions.stem: Explain why the potato firms up in distilled water.
questions.modelAnswer: Water enters the cells by osmosis down the steep gradient, the vacuoles swell and turgor pressure rises, pressing each cell against its wall so the whole potato becomes firm.

questions.stem: A student plots percentage mass change against sucrose concentration and finds the zero-crossing between two points. What does that crossing represent?
questions.modelAnswer: The concentration at which the external solution exactly matches the concentration inside the potato cells, where water would cross equally in both directions and no net change in mass would occur.

questions.stem: What does the O in CORMS require you to keep the same?

options.text: The order of the tubes
options.explanation: Order is irrelevant to the letters.

options.text: The osmotic pressure
options.explanation: Pressure is not what O stands for.

options.text: The organism — cylinders from one potato or potatoes of the same age
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: The outcome measured
options.explanation: The outcome is the M line.

questions.stem: In the osmosis investigation, what is the C line?

options.text: Changing the potato variety each time
options.explanation: The organism must stay the same.

options.text: Changing the room temperature hourly
options.explanation: Temperature is controlled, not changed.

options.text: Changing the balance used
options.explanation: The same balance should be used throughout.

options.text: Changing the concentration of the sucrose solution
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

questions.stem: Why does R call for repeats?

options.text: Repeats expose anomalous results so a reliable mean can be calculated
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: Repeats warm the solutions
options.explanation: Repeats have nothing to do with temperature.

options.text: Repeats shorten the experiment
options.explanation: They lengthen the work but raise trust.

options.text: One reading is always exactly right
options.explanation: Single readings hide anomalies.

questions.stem: Which pair fits the two M lines of the osmosis investigation?

options.text: Measure pH, after blotting
options.explanation: pH is not measured in this experiment.

options.text: Measure the change in mass, after four hours
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: Measure colour, after one week
options.explanation: Colour is the agar practical; the timing is wrong.

options.text: Measure volume, after ten minutes
options.explanation: Mass and four hours are the recorded protocol.

questions.stem: Which item belongs on the S line for this investigation?

options.text: Changing the concentration deliberately
options.explanation: That is the C line, not a control.

options.text: Timing with a different clock each run
options.explanation: Consistent timing belongs to the M line.

options.text: Controlling the volume of solution and the dimensions of each cylinder
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: Varying the blotting paper brand
options.explanation: Brand is not a controlled variable of interest.

questions.stem: State what each letter of CORMS stands for.
questions.modelAnswer: Change, Organism, Repeat, Measure, and Same — the five evaluation slots.

questions.stem: Give one example of a variable to control in the osmosis practical.
questions.modelAnswer: The volume of sucrose solution in each tube, or the dimensions of the potato cylinders.

questions.stem: Explain why the O line insists on the same potato or same-aged potatoes.
questions.modelAnswer: Because potato water content varies between tubers and ages; mixing sources would confound the mass changes with potato differences instead of isolating the effect of sucrose concentration.

questions.stem: A classmate writes 'we changed the solution and weighed the potatoes'. Rewrite it as a CORMS evaluation worth full marks.
questions.modelAnswer: C: sucrose concentration changed across six values; O: cylinders from the same potato; R: repeated three times per concentration; M1: change in mass measured; M2: after four hours; S: equal solution volumes and equal cylinder dimensions, each cylinder blotted before weighing.
